ANTM's representations of ethnic and racial identities are not as diverse as Tyra Banks would have us believe, and that the show's rhetoric of choice and diversity obscures the ways in which privilege and power operate in the fashion industry and in our society.

the ways in which the ANTM judges construct and reinforce a hegemonic, neoliberal understanding of racial and gender identities.

this paper is an examination of the ways that the reality television program America' s NextTop Model (ANTM), produced by and starring supermodel Tyra Banks, constructs and performs ethnic and gendered identity.
we have explored how the ANTM judges construct ethnic identities and how the show's rhetoric of "choice" obscures the operating of privilege.
The main takeaway from our work is that
ANTM's representations of race and gender are not only problematic but also symptomatic of a broader social phenomenon that is the neoliberal subject.

the fashion industry's aesthetic knowledge is based on a notion of "optional ethnic identity," which, while it may be "optional" for white women, is not so for women of color, who, in order to succeed in this industry, must be able to perform a variety of racialized identities, including whiteness.

the ANTM judges, in their attempts to "teach" the contestants about "real" models and "real" modeling, are actually teaching the viewers that the "real" is not only white but also "optional." This essay argues against the notion of "option" and instead suggests that ethnic and racial identities are not only not "optional" but also not "neutral" in their construction and performance.
